teaser.setup: A customer says: “We need a secure enterprise RAG assistant over our internal docs. Can you ship something in six weeks?” You're the Forward Deployed Engineer. Scope it, defend every decision, and survive the follow-ups.
you_will_practice: Turning an ambiguous customer ask into a plan
PII, security, latency, and cost constraints
Deciding what to ship in six weeks — and what to refuse to promise

sample_node.prompt: Why RAG here — why not fine-tune a model on the customer's docs?
sample_node.model: The knowledge is large, changes often, and answers must cite sources. RAG keeps facts fresh (re-index, don't retrain) and auditable. Fine-tuning teaches behavior/format, not volatile facts, and re-training on every doc change is slow and costly. Trade-off: RAG adds retrieval infrastructure and its own failure modes (bad recall, stale index).
signals: states the trade-off, not just the win

n1.prompt: The customer wants “a secure enterprise RAG assistant over internal docs” in six weeks. Before any architecture — what do you clarify first, and what is your one-paragraph approach?
n1.model: Clarify before designing: who are the users and how many; what docs and where; data sensitivity (PII/regulated?); must data stay in their cloud/region; is this Q&A only or does it take actions; latency expectation; existing IdP. Approach: a retrieval-grounded assistant — ingest+index their docs with per-document access control, answer only from retrieved context with citations, enforce the user's identity at retrieval so people only see what they're allowed to. Start read-only.

n2.prompt: Why RAG here — why not fine-tune a model on the customer's docs?
n2.model: The knowledge is large, changes often, and answers must cite sources. RAG keeps facts fresh (re-index, don't retrain) and auditable. Fine-tuning teaches behavior/format, not volatile facts, and retraining on every change is slow and costly. Trade-off: RAG adds retrieval infrastructure and its own failure modes.

n3.prompt: For retrieval, which do you propose to the customer?

n3b.prompt: That single-method choice has a known blind spot. Name it — then say what you'd add.
n3b.model: Pure vector misses exact-match terms (part numbers, error codes, policy IDs); keyword misses paraphrase and synonyms. The fix is hybrid: run both and fuse the scores, so exact terms and semantic matches both surface.
signals: names the specific failure of the chosen method

n4.prompt: You proposed hybrid. Do you also add a reranker, or just increase top-k until recall is high?
n4.model: Add a reranker. Hybrid gives good recall but noisy ordering; a cross-encoder reranker fixes precision of the top results so the model sees the best few, not just many. Just raising top-k dilutes the context, adds cost/latency, and worsens 'lost in the middle'. Trade-off: the reranker adds latency and a model to operate — skip it if the corpus is tiny or latency budget is brutal.
signals: reranker for precision, not bigger top-k
states when NOT to use it

n5.prompt: The customer's documents change every day. How do you keep retrieval fresh without rebuilding the whole index nightly?
n5.model: Incremental indexing driven by change events (or a change feed / timestamps): re-embed and upsert only changed/new docs, tombstone deletes, track provenance + version per chunk. Target an index-lag SLO (e.g. < 15 min). Full rebuilds only as a periodic safety net. Watch for embedding-model version drift — if you change models you must re-embed everything.

n6.prompt: The customer asks: “How will you know retrieval is actually good?” What's your evaluation plan?
n6.model: Build a small labeled eval set of real questions → known-relevant docs. Measure retrieval separately from answer quality: recall@k and MRR/nDCG for retrieval; groundedness/citation-accuracy for answers. Run it in CI so a chunking/model/top-k change is a measurable regression, not a vibe. Expand the set from real logged misses.
signals: separates retrieval eval from answer eval

n7.prompt: How do you detect and reduce hallucination — and what do you do when retrieval returns nothing relevant?
n7.model: Constrain the model to answer only from retrieved context and cite the chunks; if nothing relevant is retrieved, return 'I don't have that' rather than fabricate. Detect with groundedness checks (is each claim supported by a citation?) and an eval metric. A no-answer is a retrieval bug to fix (index/query/top-k), not a prompt to loosen. Log misses.
signals: treats no-answer as a retrieval bug

n8.prompt: Two weeks in, the customer's security team refuses to give you production credentials or access to real documents. Now what?
n8.model: This is normal in FDE work — don't stall. Work against a representative sample or synthetic docs the customer approves; agree on a data-handling boundary (their cloud/VPC, no egress). Build the pipeline so credentials are injected at their environment, not held by you: least-privilege service accounts, secrets in their manager, you deliver code + IaC they run. Define a joint test plan they execute inside their boundary. Never ask them to lower security for your convenience.
signals: shifts creds/secrets into the customer's boundary
delivers deployable artifacts, not your-laptop access
doesn't ask them to weaken security

n9.prompt: The corpus contains employee PII and HR documents. How do you prevent one user from seeing another's data through the assistant?
n9.model: Enforce access at retrieval, not after: carry the user's identity (via their IdP/SSO) into the query and filter to documents that user is allowed to see (per-doc/row ACLs). You can't leak what you never retrieve. Add an output DLP scan for PII/secrets as defense in depth, classify + mask sensitive fields, and audit every retrieval. Treat retrieved text as data, not instructions (indirect injection).
signals: per-user ACL AT retrieval, not post-filter

n10.prompt: The customer wants it to “feel instant.” What latency target do you commit to, and how?
n10.model: Commit to a perceived-latency target, not a single number: stream tokens so first-token < ~1s, full answer in a few seconds. Levers: cache the fixed system/context prefix (prompt caching), cache frequent Q&A, keep the reranker to a small candidate set, right-size the model for the hot path and escalate only hard queries. Measure per-hop latency (retrieval vs rerank vs model) so you optimize the actual bottleneck. Don't promise a hard p99 before you've measured under their load.
signals: won't commit a number before measuring

n11.prompt: Finance asks what this will cost to run and how you'll keep it from exploding. Answer.
n11.model: Give a cost model: requests/day × avg tokens × per-token price, minus cache-hit rate, plus embedding + rerank + vector-store cost. Levers: route easy queries to a cheaper model, prompt-cache the fixed prefix, cap max tokens, dedupe/cache frequent questions, right-size top-k. Put a budget alert + per-request cost telemetry in place so a spike is visible and attributable. Don't let cost be discovered on the invoice.

n12.prompt: You shipped. One morning the customer says answer quality “suddenly got worse” overnight — nothing was deployed. Walk your debugging.
n12.model: Isolate the layer, cheap things first. Overnight + no deploy points at data/index: did an ingestion job run and re-embed with a different/upgraded embedding model (dimension or version drift), leaving the query and index in different spaces? Did a bulk doc update tombstone/replace chunks or change ACLs so retrieval now returns less? Check: retrieval metrics (recall@k) vs yesterday, index freshness/version, embedding-model version, and a few known queries' retrieved chunks. Mitigate: pin/rollback the embedding model and re-embed consistently; add a version guard so query and index models must match. It's almost always retrieval, not the LLM.
signals: checks recall@k vs baseline + retrieved chunks

n13.prompt: It's a six-week engagement. What do you actually commit to shipping in that window?
n13.model: Ship the smallest thing that delivers real value and proves the architecture: ingestion + incremental index for the top document sources, hybrid retrieval + reranker, answer-from-context with citations, SSO + per-user ACL at retrieval, a small eval set in CI, basic observability (latency/cost/retrieval quality), read-only (no write actions yet). Explicitly defer: actions/tool-use, every edge-case source, multi-language, fancy UI. A working, secure, evaluated slice beats a broad demo.
signals: a narrow, secure, evaluated vertical slice

n14.prompt: The customer pushes for guarantees. What do you refuse to promise — and how do you say it?
n14.model: Refuse to promise: 100% accuracy / zero hallucination; a hard latency p99 before load testing in their environment; that it can take write actions safely in six weeks; that it covers every document source day one. Say it as scope, not weakness: 'I won't promise zero hallucination — no one honestly can — but I will promise citations on every answer, an eval gate, and a measured groundedness number you can hold me to.' Trading a fake guarantee for a real, measurable commitment is the senior move.
signals: refuses fake guarantees (accuracy, hard p99, safe writes in 6wk)

n15.prompt: Rate how you defended this end-to-end. Where did you hand-wave instead of naming a mechanism and a trade-off?
checklist: I enforced per-user access AT retrieval
I had an evaluation plan, not vibes
I kept momentum when blocked on credentials
I named cost + latency levers with telemetry
I debugged the incident by isolating layers
I scoped six weeks honestly and refused fake guarantees

n16.prompt: Strong work. Keep the pressure on with a related drill:

recommend.label: The Interviewer Keeps Asking Why — RAG chain
